approach:
To begin this lesson, put the terms 'ante meridiem' and 'post meridiem' in front of the class. Ask them to discuss what they think these terms might mean. Tell them that meridiem has something to do with midday. Let them discuss this and continue to drop hints until they arrive at the idea that a.m. and p.m. come from the Latin words for 'before midday' and 'after midday'.
Now show students the Explore task and let them discuss the question with one another. Ask them how they would write 08:15 in the morning. What would the hour hand look like at that time? Why? Where would the minute hand be? Why? Show them Master 2 and allow them to discuss their thoughts.
During Guided Practice, students are looking at pictorial clues and determining whether it is 'a.m.' or 'p.m.'

approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with clocks. Then show them the Explore task and ask them if they can replicate the time shown in the picture on their own clock. What time does the clock show? How do they know? How can they be sure? Count on together with students in fives starting from 9 o'clock to 9:20, and then count on in 1-minute intervals until 9:24. Tell them your friend says that if you count up all of the small markings you get to 60. Is this true? What does the 60 stand for?
Next, ask students what they notice about the hour hand on their clocks as they move the minute hand. Is there a relationship or does the hour hand just switch numbers at the end of 60 minutes? Allow them to discuss with their partners how the hour hand moves within a period of an hour. For example, when the minute hand shows half past, the hour hand is halfway between hours. Show students the images in Master 3 and 4, and then ask them to describe the positions of the hour hands and explain the difference.
During Guided Practice, students are telling time to the minute. Ask them how they can tell the time to the minute without counting every small marking.

objective: tell and write the time from 12-hour and 24-hour clocks.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the digital clock from the Explore task and ask them what time the digital clock is showing. Tell them your friend said it is showing 13 minutes. Is this correct? How can we be sure? Allow students time to discuss what the watch is showing. Then tell them you think it might be showing 1 o'clock in the afternoon because if you continue counting after 12 noon, 1 o'clock would be 13. Is this true? (Master 1.) What would the other times be?
Show students the Explore picture and ask them to talk to their partners about the times shown. Can they tell you at what time the movie 'Coz and Dot' starts? (Master 2) Show them Master 3 and 4, and allow them time to discuss. Is 'Treble C' starting in the morning or evening? What about 'Super Cooper'? How do you know? Ask them, if they need to get into the theatre 15 minutes before the movie begins, what time should they be in by? Impress upon students that when using the 24-hour clock, there is no need to indicate a.m. and p.m.
During Guided Practice, students are writing digital times as a.m. or p.m. and then describing the time using prompts. Ask them if they notice a relationship between the words 'to' and 'past' and the minutes shown (e.g. 1–30 are 'past' and 31–59 are 'to').

lesson_title: Measuring and Comparing Time in Seconds
objective: measure and compare time in seconds.
approach:
To begin this lesson, ask students to work in pairs to complete an activity with a stopwatch. Ask them to set it to countdown from 20 seconds. Alternatively, use an online countdown timer for the whole class. Ask students to focus on how long 20 seconds is.
First, ask students to find out how many times they can clap in 20 seconds. Then ask them what other activities they could try to do in 20 seconds. Show them the activities suggested in Master. Help them to draw a table to record the time it takes for each activity. Introduce the abbreviation 's' for seconds. Work through the Master tasks with students and complete the chart. During Master 4, ask students what other activities they think could be completed in the same time it took the swimmers to swim 50 m.
Remind students that the digits to the right of the seconds indicate part of a second. They will learn about this in future year groups.
Students may have the opportunity to use analogue stopwatches. Show them a stopwatch that has started and ask them to decide what the increments stand for. Agree that the stopwatch is showing the time in seconds. Tell students that they will be learning why it is labelled to 60 in future lessons. There may be students who know that 60 seconds is equal to 1 minute.
During Guided Practice, students are looking at the time on a stopwatch and comparing time in seconds.

read the time in seconds on a stopwatch (digital clock).
Students can measure activity lengths in seconds.

approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with a stopwatch and ask them to record the amount of time it takes them to draw a rectangle accurately using a ruler. Record the times for them. Guide them to see that the same distance walked by different people will take different amounts of time.
Show the class Master 1 and discuss what is shown on the stopwatch and the phone stopwatch. Ask them to read the times shown. Guide them to see how seconds are displayed in digital form. Ask students to discuss who took longer to draw a rectangle and by how much.
Next, show them Master 2 and ask them to guess how long it took Holly to get across the playground. Tell them your friend said it took Holly 14 minutes to get across the playground. Is this true? How else can we know that this is not correct? (Is it reasonable to think that it would take someone 14 minutes to get across the playground?)
During Guided Practice, students are reading stopwatches to tell the time in seconds.

approach:
To begin the lesson, show students an analogue clock with a second hand. Ask them to look at the second hand and compare it with the hour and minute hands. How can we differentiate the second hand from the minute and hour hands? Show students how to read time using the second hand. Guide them to realise that the measurement in seconds using the analogue clock is the same for the minute hand and second hand, and then ask them to count in seconds using the clock face. They can count in blocks of 5 seconds.
Then use the clock to conduct an experiment to count how many times students can deal a pack of cards in 15 seconds. Students should use the second hand on the clock to measure 15 seconds. Divide students into two groups; one group will focus on watching the time, and the other group will count the number of cards dealt. One card dealt is counted when the card is placed in front of the student. Complete the experiment four times with the groups switching roles each time. Write down the number of cards dealt for each experiment, and then compare the results. The time remains the same, but what about the number of cards dealt? Discuss the results with the class.
During Guided Practice, students are comparing elapsed time in a series of experiments.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Allow them to talk about how much time has passed by looking at the pictures of the clocks. After they have discussed this, tell them your friend said that because the minute hand has not moved, you only need to count the hours that have passed. Is this true? Is there a way we can check? Ask students what time might look like if we were to place it on a timeline. Is this a helpful tool to see how much time has passed? What intervals would be helpful to mark on a timeline: 5 minutes or 15 minutes? What might it depend on? Prompt them to use the timeline in different ways, using the examples from Master.
During Guided Practice, students are using multiple methods to calculate the passage of time. Help them to discover multiple ways of calculating how much time has passed, and ask them which one is most appropriate for each example. Also ask them to suggest activities for each example bearing in mind the number of hours.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and allow them to use an analogue clock to help solve the problem. Guide students to see that the problem requires us to count backwards to find the starting time. Ask them to determine the time on the clock, and then show students how to count backwards in hourly intervals, from 2:10 p.m., then 1:10 p.m., 12:10 p.m., 11:10 a.m. to 10:10 a.m. Ask students if they are able to show 4 hours ago on a timeline. What would that look like? Will the minutes change when you move backwards by 1 full hour? Why, or why not?
What if Tama and his mum took 3 hours and 30 minutes rather than 4 hours? How would that change the starting time? Ask students to use the timeline to show what time they would have started.

approach:

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and allow them to work on this problem. Ask them how many minutes it takes to reach 2:00 p.m. from 1:40 p.m. Show them that the 45-minute duration can be broken up into 20 minutes and 25 minutes using a number bond. Draw the timeline to show 1:40 p.m. to 2:00 p.m., then add 25 minutes to 2:25 p.m. The girls stopped playing at 2:25 p.m. Guide students to see that counting minutes to the next hour, then counting on to find the ending time, is a method of counting time.
What if the girls started at 1:30 p.m. instead of 1:40 p.m.? Get students to calculate the ending time using the method above. How many minutes does it take to make the next hour? How many minutes are left from the duration? Ask them to count on to find the ending time.
During Guided Practice, students are calculating the ending time given the starting time and duration of activities. Ask them to think of activities that take approximately the same amounts of time.

approach:
To begin this lesson, ask students how much the second hand moves in 1 minute. Allow them to observe the second hand for 1 minute. The second hand would have moved 1 complete turn in 1 minute. Ask them how many seconds do they think there are in 1 minute? Since the second hand moved 1 complete turn in 1 minute, we can tell that in 1 minute, there are 60 seconds. Then ask them how we could calculate the number of seconds in 5 minutes. If 1 minute = 60 seconds then 5 minutes = 5 × 60 = 300 seconds.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and allow them to solve this problem using multiple methods. Tell them your friend sees the 6 times table in 180 seconds and that helps him solve the problem. However, another friend says she can use number bonds to help her solve the problem. How would this work? In which way would we want to break up the number of seconds: by 100, 10 or 60? Why is this?
As demonstrated in the Master tasks, provide students with the different lengths of time they will need to turn into minutes and seconds. The focus of using number bonds needs to be in pulling out 60 seconds as many times as possible to determine the number of minutes. Ask them to explore why this is — why not use smaller intervals? Could we use smaller intervals like 30 seconds? Encourage students to demonstrate using multiple methods to solve problems.
During Guided Practice, students are using number bonds to break apart a number of seconds.

objective: find the number of days in each month, year and leap year.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and tell them your friend said it was impossible they had their birthdays on the last day of the month as all months have the same number of days. Is this true? How can they find out? Which months have 30 days? Which months have more than 30 days? Are there any months that have fewer days?
Show students Master 3 and ask them to name the years that have 28 days in February and those years that have 29 days. Do they know what to call a year in which February has 29 days? It is called a 'leap year'. Ask students to study the table. How often does a 'leap year' occur? Ask them to count the number of days in a year that is not a 'leap year'. Explain to students that a leap year is any year that is divisible by 4. However if a year is divisible by 100, it also needs to be divisible by 400 to be a leap year. So 1900, even though it is divisible by 4, is not a leap year.
During Guided Practice, students are calculating the number of days it took to complete certain activities. In the second example, allow them time to work out the answer as there are multiple solutions depending on when Ravi's dad went away, and if it is a 'leap year' or not. Prompt them as necessary.
The traditional Māori lunar calendar, maramataka, begins in June/July. Historically, the calendar recorded the movements of the moon rather than the movements of the sun throughout the year. Students may be given the opportunity to look at the differences and similarities and recognise that while maramataka has 12 months, they do not align perfectly with the months used in Lessons 19 and 20.

objective: find the duration in terms of number of days.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask them how many ways they can show the number of days in Ravi's camping trip. Tell them your friend said if you subtract 5 from 18 you get 13, so that must mean the camping trip was only 13 days long. Is this correct? What has the friend not counted?
Ask students how they can prove this using the monthly calendar. Then ask them what if the camping trip only lasted for 10 days, when would it end? Tell them your friend said if you add 10 to 5 you get 15, so it must end on the 15th. Is this correct? Has the friend made the same mistake? How can we use a calendar to check our answer? Ask students to discuss why you cannot use simple addition or subtraction to solve the calendar questions.
During Guided Practice, students are using calendars to solve problems related to the duration of days.
